TOPIC 01Closures / Mergers

The College Closure Wave: Which Schools Are Vulnerable and How to Protect Your Student

At least 16 nonprofit colleges closed in 2025. More than 80 have closed or merged in five years. The pace is accelerating in 2026. Here is how to assess risk before it affects your student.

University Business and Higher Ed Dive are tracking a growing list of college closures in 2026. Labouré College of Healthcare in Massachusetts is closing, with Curry College absorbing its nursing programs. Lourdes University in Ohio is closing due to declining enrollment and financial pressure. California College of the Arts cited enrollment troubles, accreditation issues, and rising costs. The pattern is consistent: small, tuition-dependent institutions with multi-year enrollment declines and no endowment cushion.

Only 47% of students who experience a college closure ultimately re-enroll in another program. The merger wave is also accelerating: Washington University in St. Louis is absorbing Fontbonne University. Pomona College is in exclusive negotiations to acquire Claremont Graduate University. These combinations can be healthy — but they also change the character of institutions mid-enrollment.

🎓 Elite Institution Spotlight
The Pomona-Claremont Merger: What Elite Liberal Arts Consolidation Looks Like
Pomona College
Ranked among the top 5 liberal arts colleges in the U.S.; its acquisition of Claremont Graduate University would give it a graduate school component for the first time.
Claremont McKenna / Harvey Mudd
The other Claremont Consortium members are watching carefully; a Pomona-CGU merger could reshape the balance of the entire consortium.
Williams / Amherst / Bowdoin
The closure and merger wave has not reached the top liberal arts colleges — but smaller liberal arts schools in New England are facing genuine enrollment pressure.
Grinnell / Oberlin / DePauw
Mid-tier liberal arts colleges face more acute pressure than the top 20; these schools' enrollment trends and financial health deserve scrutiny if they're on your list.
Not all mergers are distress signals. When a top-5 liberal arts college absorbs a graduate university, it can create a stronger institution for enrolled students. The key questions: who is driving the merger, what financial guarantees exist, and what happens to specific programs your student is considering?
Dr. Hurwitz's Take
I tell every family I work with: school stability is a non-negotiable factor in the college selection process. A school that closes or dramatically restructures while your student is enrolled is not just an inconvenience — it can derail four years of plans, cost money you can't recover, and in the worst cases leave students without a degree and with debt. Before committing to any school, look at five years of enrollment data, ask about financial reserves, and check accreditation status on the CHEA database.
Potential Benefits
  • Mergers, when done well, preserve missions while improving financial stability
  • Strong schools acquiring weaker ones can benefit both
  • Students at closing schools have legal protections including teach-out plans
Key Concerns
  • Only 47% of students at closed schools re-enroll anywhere
  • Credits may not transfer, costing students time and money
  • Institutional character changes significantly when schools merge mid-enrollment
Key Articles This Week
  • University Business — 'Tracking College Closings in Higher Ed 2026'
  • Inside Higher Ed — 'Colleges That Couldn't Survive 2025'
  • BestColleges — 'Closed Colleges: List of Closures, Mergers, and Trendline'
✓ Your Action Checklist
  • Check the CHEA database (chea.org) for accreditation status of every school on your list
  • Review 3–5 year enrollment trends — look for multi-year declines
  • Ask directly: has your school had financial exigency declarations or accreditation warnings?
  • For small schools under 2,000 students: ask about endowment size and financial reserves
❓ Questions to Ask Admissions
  • 'What is your institutional endowment size relative to your annual operating budget?'
  • 'Has your school received any accreditation warnings in the past five years?'
  • 'Do you have a teach-out agreement with another institution in case of closure?'

TOPIC 02Legal / Federal Policy

Five Lawsuits That Will Define Higher Education in 2026

The Trump administration is at the center of the most consequential legal battles in higher education in decades. The outcomes will shape the sector for a generation.

Higher Ed Dive published its authoritative roundup of five major higher education lawsuits to watch in 2026. The Harvard case is the most watched: Harvard sued over the $2.2 billion funding freeze, winning a ruling from Judge Allison Burroughs that the administration violated Harvard's First Amendment rights. The AAUP has filed separate suits over actions against Harvard, Columbia, and the University of California, winning standing and favorable rulings in both.

The cumulative pattern: courts are consistently ruling against the administration on procedural and constitutional grounds. But the administration continues to act, accept rulings, and find new avenues. Legal victories do not produce stability — they produce a different version of ongoing litigation.

Dr. Hurwitz's Take
I follow these lawsuits carefully because the outcomes shape the environment every student will inhabit at a research university. The pattern so far — administration overreaches, courts block it, administration finds a new angle — tells me this is a multi-year battle that won't be resolved before your student enrolls. Choose institutions that are managing this uncertainty well, not ones lurching between crises.
Potential Benefits
  • Courts have consistently blocked unlawful funding freezes on First Amendment grounds
  • AAUP legal victories extend protections beyond Harvard to other institutions
  • Congressional appropriations are blocking some administrative overreach
Key Concerns
  • Legal uncertainty creates hiring and planning freezes that harm academic quality
  • Each victory triggers a new administrative action — no stable resolution in sight
  • Ongoing litigation consumes institutional resources and leadership attention
Key Articles This Week
  • Higher Ed Dive — '5 Higher Ed Lawsuits to Watch in 2026'
  • Harvard Independent — 'A Year of Cuts: Harvard and Columbia's Federal Funding Fight'
  • Science/AAAS — 'Appeals Court Agrees NIH Cannot Reduce Overhead Payments'
✓ Your Action Checklist
  • Track Harvard lawsuit outcomes — they set precedents affecting all research universities
  • For research-focused students: ask about grant stability at the lab level
  • Look for schools whose presidents are communicating clearly and confidently about legal challenges
❓ Questions to Ask Admissions
  • 'How is your institution's legal situation with federal funding affecting your hiring and planning?'
  • 'What is your presidential communication strategy around the federal funding battles?'
  • 'Has any litigation outcome meaningfully changed your institution's financial situation?'

TOPIC 03Mental Health / Loneliness

The Loneliness Epidemic: More Than Half of College Students Feel Disconnected

A landmark study of 65,000 students at 120 colleges finds more than half report feeling lonely. The mental health picture on campus is more complex — and more concerning — than headlines capture.

A new study in the Journal of American College Health, examining data from nearly 65,000 students across more than 120 colleges, confirmed that more than half of U.S. college students report feeling lonely. Lead researcher Professor Sasha Zhou identified social media use above two hours daily as a significant correlate of loneliness. For a population at the age of onset for lifetime mental illness — 75% of lifetime mental illness presents by age 24 — adding chronic loneliness creates 'a really concerning situation.'

The good news: the Healthy Minds Study of 84,000 students found that severe depression rates have declined three years running, to 18% from 23% in 2022. But loneliness may be the next wave of concern even as diagnosed mental illness rates stabilize.

🎓 Elite Institution Spotlight
Mental Health Infrastructure at Elite Universities: Who's Getting It Right
Yale
Created a major mental health initiative; now employs embedded counselors in residential colleges — one of the better-designed systems in the country.
Stanford
Has expanded mental health support substantially; wait times have decreased but remain a student concern in peak periods.
Duke
Introduced the 'DukeReach' proactive outreach model, identifying at-risk students before crisis using early warning data.
University of Michigan
Runs the Healthy Minds Study and has used its own data to improve campus resources; strong peer support infrastructure.
For families with students who have mental health needs or histories, the specific mental health infrastructure at a college is as important as the academic program. The difference between a school with embedded residential counselors and proactive outreach versus one with a standalone counseling center with 6-week wait times is enormous in practice.
Dr. Hurwitz's Take
Mental health is now one of the most important factors I ask families to evaluate in a school. Ask specifically about wait times, not just the existence of services. A counseling center that takes six weeks to see a student in crisis is not a mental health resource. The schools getting this right have embedded mental health support in residence halls and advising.
Potential Benefits
  • Depression and anxiety rates declining for third consecutive year
  • Some campuses are embedding mental health support in residential and academic settings
  • Peer support programs are proving effective at reaching at-risk students
Key Concerns
  • More than half of students report feeling lonely — a direct risk factor for mental illness
  • Social media use is replacing in-person connection
  • Many counseling centers have wait times that make timely care inaccessible
Key Articles This Week
  • WBUR/Here & Now — 'College Students Mental Health'
  • University of Michigan — Healthy Minds Study 2024-2025
  • Inside Higher Ed — 'College Student Mental Health Remains a Wicked Problem'
✓ Your Action Checklist
  • Ask about counseling center wait times — not just whether services exist
  • Research whether target schools have embedded mental health support beyond a standalone counseling center
  • Ask current students about the mental health culture on campus
❓ Questions to Ask Admissions
  • 'What is the average wait time to see a counselor at your mental health center?'
  • 'Do you have embedded counselors in residence halls or academic departments?'
  • 'What programs does your campus offer specifically to address student loneliness and social connection?'

TOPIC 04FAFSA / Financial Aid

FAFSA Completions Double in Autumn: The Single Best News in Financial Aid Policy This Year

The earlier September FAFSA release has doubled autumn completion rates. This is a genuine win that families should act on immediately — but a two-speed system is forming.

Federal Student Aid reported that FAFSA completions for the Class of 2026 are outpacing last year's at every demographic category measured. The doubling of autumn FAFSA submissions is a direct result of the earlier September availability window. Many institutional aid programs are first-come, first-served. Students who file in September are evaluated for merit and need-based aid simultaneously — and they have more time to understand their options.

The troubling pattern: the families most likely to file early are the families least likely to need the earliest aid. A critical finding: 44% of students who would need private loans to bridge the gap between federal limits and actual costs have credit scores too low to qualify for those private loans. This means many students believe they have a backup financing option they will not actually be able to access.

🎓 Elite Institution Spotlight
Elite Schools and FAFSA: What 'Meets 100% of Need' Actually Means in Practice
MIT
Meets 100% of demonstrated need; no loans in aid packages for families under $140K income. FAFSA is the gateway to these awards.
Harvard
Meets 100% of need; families earning under $85K pay nothing. Families under $150K pay no more than 10% of income.
Yale
Similar to Harvard; comprehensive need-based program that cannot be activated without a FAFSA on file.
Pomona / Swarthmore / Williams
Top liberal arts colleges with similar policies. Often less well-known for financial generosity than the Ivies — but equally compelling.
Filing FAFSA to access elite school aid is not just for low-income families. A family earning $175,000 with two children in college simultaneously may qualify for substantial need-based aid. The only way to know is to file.
Dr. Hurwitz's Take
If I could give every family in America one piece of college planning advice, it would be this: file the FAFSA in September, every year, no matter what you think your income is. I have worked with families earning $180,000 who received substantial institutional grants from elite schools that required FAFSA data for evaluation. File it early. File it every year.
Potential Benefits
  • Earlier September availability creates better planning timeline for families
  • First-come, first-served aid programs reward early filers significantly
  • Elite school need-based programs cannot be accessed without FAFSA on file
Key Concerns
  • 49% of eligible non-filers still think they won't qualify — massive outreach failure
  • Rolling aid creates a system that disadvantages less-informed families
  • 44% of students who need private loans may not qualify — a critical unplanned gap
Key Articles This Week
  • NASFAA Legislative Conference — FAFSA Completion Data
  • Detroit News — 'How Student Loans and Financial Aid Are Changing in 2026'
  • T. Rowe Price — 'How New Education Policies Could Change Financial Aid'
✓ Your Action Checklist
  • Mark September 2026 on your calendar NOW as FAFSA filing date — don't wait
  • Complete FAFSA regardless of income assumptions
  • Check your family's credit score now if you plan to use private loans to bridge a financing gap
  • Research which institutional aid programs at your target schools are rolling vs. priority deadline
❓ Questions to Ask Admissions
  • 'Does your school meet 100% of demonstrated financial need?'
  • 'What is your priority FAFSA deadline for institutional aid consideration?'
  • 'Are any of your grant or scholarship programs rolling, and when do they typically become fully committed?'

TOPIC 05Future of Higher Education

Eleven Scholars Predict 2026 Is a Turning Point for American Higher Education

The Chronicle assembled 11 leading thinkers to predict higher education's future. The consensus: 2026 is the year that separates leaders who understand the moment from those who don't.

The Chronicle of Higher Education's landmark 2026 Trends Report assembled 11 leading scholars, administrators, and policy analysts. The consensus is that 2026 represents a genuine inflection point. As NYU's Clay Shirky writes: institutions that fail to recognize the convergence of AI disruption, demographic change, and political pressure 'will be forced into painful restructuring, mergers, or closures.' Alondra Nelson argues that 'colleges and universities will become a primary site of democratic contestation over artificial intelligence.'

The line that resonates most: 'Ten years from now, we will look back on 2026 as the year when we could distinguish the leaders who understood what time it was from those who did not.'

🎓 Elite Institution Spotlight
Elite University Presidents and the 'Turning Point' Test
Harvard — Alan Garber
Has been admirably clear and public about the stakes of the federal battle; his willingness to fight rather than settle signals an understanding of what the moment requires for academic freedom.
MIT — Sally Kornbluth
Has been strategic and vocal about federal research funding threats; MIT's early legal positioning and public communications have been among the clearest in the sector.
Columbia — Katrina Armstrong
Columbia's settlement decision remains the most contested presidential choice of the year; whether it was the right call will be debated for a decade.
Princeton — Christopher Eisgruber
Has maintained a quiet but firm posture; Princeton's financial cushion gives Eisgruber the luxury of patience that other presidents don't have.
The quality of presidential leadership is now a legitimate college selection criterion. Presidents who understand the moment — who are clear, decisive, and focused on protecting the academic mission — are running better institutions. This is a management and institutional quality observation, not a partisan one.
Dr. Hurwitz's Take
I read the Chronicle's 11 scholars piece carefully, and that line stays with me. It applies to families too. The families who treat the next four years as business as usual — who choose a college based on prestige rankings alone, who don't ask about institutional financial health, who don't evaluate career readiness, who don't understand how AI is changing the value proposition of a degree — will be disadvantaged. The families who understand what time it is will navigate this exceptionally well.
Potential Benefits
  • Genuine leader institutions are responding thoughtfully to all these challenges
  • Academic freedom remains a core institutional value defended vigorously by most institutions
  • AI disruption creates opportunities for pedagogical innovation alongside its risks
Key Concerns
  • Institutions that don't understand the moment will harm students through reactive choices
  • AI disruption timeline may outpace institutional capacity to adapt
  • The sector is unlikely to shrink in an orderly way — affected students will bear real costs
Key Articles This Week
  • Chronicle of Higher Education — 'Higher Education Is at a Turning Point. 11 Scholars Predict What's Next'
  • Chronicle of Higher Education — 'The Trends Report 2026'
✓ Your Action Checklist
  • Ask schools: how is your leadership thinking about AI, demographic change, and financial pressure together?
  • Look for schools whose presidents are writing and speaking publicly about these challenges
  • Choose institutions whose strategic planning accounts for the current moment rather than assuming business as usual
❓ Questions to Ask Admissions
  • 'How is your institution's strategic plan addressing AI disruption, demographic decline, and financial pressure simultaneously?'
  • 'What does your president say publicly about the future of your institution?'
  • 'In ten years, what will distinguish the institutions that thrived through this period?'

TOPIC 06Research Funding / Congressional

Congress Locks In NIH Funding Protections: A Rare Win for Research Universities

Congress quietly tucked language into a spending bill that bars the administration from changing how NIH calculates indirect cost reimbursements — converting a court victory into a statutory protection.

Congress embedded language in a package of spending bills that bars the administration from changing how NIH and other federal agencies calculate indirect cost reimbursements for the remainder of the fiscal year. This converts what had been a court-ordered protection into a statutory one — a significantly stronger and more durable form of protection. The NIH indirect cost cap — which would have imposed a flat 15% reimbursement rate, potentially costing the sector $5.2 billion annually — is now blocked both by court order and by law.

The Trump administration still has until April 6 to decide whether to appeal to the Supreme Court. Even if it does, the Congressional statutory language provides a separate line of defense.

🎓 Elite Institution Spotlight
NIH Funding at Top Research Universities: What the Protection Means in Practice
Johns Hopkins University
Receives more NIH funding than any other institution — over $800M annually. The indirect cost protection is not abstract for Hopkins: it protects an operating model built around federal research revenue.
University of Michigan
Among the top 5 NIH recipients; has maintained research operations despite the uncertain environment by moving quickly to diversify grant sources.
Duke University Medical Center
Research funding supports a significant portion of Duke's overall operating budget; the statutory protection provides planning stability the institution urgently needed.
Vanderbilt / Emory / Georgetown
Mid-tier research universities with significant NIH exposure; for these schools, the indirect cost protection matters more proportionally than it does for Hopkins or Michigan.
The NIH indirect cost battle is not primarily an undergraduate issue — it affects graduate students and research faculty most directly. But for families whose students plan research careers, the stability of a university's research infrastructure is a legitimate factor in graduate program selection. Ask specifically about a program's grant status, not just the university's overall financial health.
Dr. Hurwitz's Take
I want to be careful not to oversell this victory. Congressional language in an annual spending bill is real protection — but it's protection for this fiscal year. The administration could still appeal to the Supreme Court. And grant terminations on antisemitism grounds continue independently. The honest message: the research infrastructure at major universities is more protected today than it appeared three months ago. Meaningful — but not a permanent resolution.
Potential Benefits
  • Statutory protection is stronger than court orders alone
  • Bipartisan vote signals congressional support for research university funding
  • $415M NIH increase protects biomedical research capacity
Key Concerns
  • Protection is only for current fiscal year — may not extend to 2027
  • Administration may still appeal to Supreme Court
  • Grant terminations on antisemitism grounds are a separate ongoing issue
Key Articles This Week
  • Chronicle of Higher Education — 'How Higher Ed Staved Off a Research-Funding Bloodbath — For Now'
  • ACE — 'House Passes FY 2026 Spending Package'
  • Science/AAAS — Indirect Cost Legal Coverage
✓ Your Action Checklist
  • Research universities are more financially stable than January headlines suggested — update your assessment
  • For STEM-focused graduate students: ask about specific lab funding status, not just institutional health
  • Monitor April 6 — the administration's Supreme Court appeal deadline
❓ Questions to Ask Admissions
  • 'Has your institution's federal research funding situation stabilized following recent Congressional and court actions?'
  • 'For specific labs: are there active grants funding the research your student would join?'
  • 'What is your long-term strategy for protecting research funding regardless of federal policy?'

TOPIC 07State Funding / Tuition

State Budget Cuts Are Coming for Public Universities — and Students Will Feel Them

Oregon, Florida, Kansas, and multiple other states are advancing tuition increases and budget cuts at public universities. The affordable public option is becoming less affordable.

Oregon State University raised tuition over 6% for new students. The Florida Board of Governors approved a 12% tuition increase at four-year institutions. Kansas House committee legislation would significantly cut state funding for public universities. These decisions are happening in parallel with federal funding uncertainty — creating a double squeeze for institutions that depend on both state and federal revenue.

The practical implication for families: the net cost of public universities — after accounting for tuition increases, reduced institutional aid, and service cuts — may be higher in 2026–27 than families calculated when building their college list. Do not assume that the public university option is automatically cheaper than the private college option.

🎓 Elite Institution Spotlight
Public Flagship vs. Private Peer: The Value Calculation Is Changing
UT Austin vs. Rice University
UT Austin's 12% tuition increase and ongoing curriculum legislation pressure makes the net-cost comparison with Rice — a top-15 university with strong need-based aid — more favorable to Rice than ever.
University of Michigan vs. Northwestern
Michigan in-state remains exceptional value. Michigan out-of-state (~$56K) now approaches Northwestern's net price for many families — and Northwestern meets 100% of demonstrated need.
UCLA / UC Berkeley vs. USC
UCLA and UC Berkeley are still exceptional values for California residents. For out-of-state students, USC's merit scholarships make it competitive on net cost — check both before assuming the UC is cheaper.
University of Florida vs. University of Miami
UF is still dramatically cheaper for Florida residents. For out-of-state students considering Florida, the state's legislative climate makes Miami more attractive on a complete value basis.
The most common mistake I see families make is assuming public = affordable and private = expensive. In the current environment, net cost comparisons are often surprising in favor of private institutions — especially for strong students who qualify for merit aid. Run the numbers before assuming.
Dr. Hurwitz's Take
I tell families this every year, and it has never been more true: do not assume that the public university option is automatically cheaper than the private college option. Run the net price calculators. A private college that offers $35,000 in merit and need-based aid may be cheaper than a public university at full out-of-state rates — and the public university option is now getting more expensive faster than it has in years.
Potential Benefits
  • In-state public options remain among the most affordable for in-state residents
  • Some states are protecting higher education budgets despite federal uncertainty
Key Concerns
  • Tuition increases outpacing inflation at many public universities
  • State budget cuts reduce services and increase class sizes
  • Out-of-state public tuition often exceeds private college net price
Key Articles This Week
  • Inside Higher Ed — Southern Oregon University Budget Coverage
  • Higher Ed Dive — Florida and Oregon Tuition Coverage
✓ Your Action Checklist
  • Run updated net price calculations for all public universities on your list — tuition increases may have changed the math
  • Compare public out-of-state vs. private college net costs directly
  • Ask public universities: what services or programs have been cut in response to budget pressure?
❓ Questions to Ask Admissions
  • 'Has your state legislature approved any tuition increases for the 2026-27 academic year?'
  • 'What programs or services have been reduced due to budget pressure?'
  • 'Is your institutional aid locked for four years or subject to annual adjustment?'

Guidance Counselor Corner

What Every Counselor Should Know and Share This Week

Seven major developments this week. Most actionable for counselors: First, the FAFSA Spotlight maps exactly what 'meets 100% of need' looks like at Harvard, MIT, Yale, and top liberal arts colleges — this is practical information families can use to recalibrate their college lists. Second, the Eleven Scholars Spotlight maps which elite university presidents seem to understand the moment — this is now a legitimate institutional quality criterion that counselors can reference when advising about school selection. Third, the State Budget Spotlight maps specific school comparisons (UT Austin vs. Rice, Michigan vs. Northwestern) that show how the net cost calculation has shifted. Help families run comparative net price calculations rather than making sticker-price assumptions.

The closure wave is continuing — the Pomona-Claremont merger analysis explains what a healthy elite merger looks like versus a distress signal, which is practical information for counselors advising students at smaller liberal arts colleges.

What This Means For Families

Your Action Guide — Edition 2026-05

Dr. Hurwitz's Analysis · January 26–30, 2026

Here is what this week's news means in practical terms — and what your family should do about it right now.

🏫
Check school stability before committing
Use the CHEA database (chea.org) to verify accreditation status. Ask about enrollment trends and financial reserves. A school that closes during your student's enrollment is the worst possible outcome.
📅
September FAFSA is most critical at schools ranked 20–150
At schools that meet 100% of need regardless of filing date (Harvard, MIT, Yale), timing matters less. At schools with rolling merit aid, September filing is a significant financial advantage.
👑
Presidential leadership is now a college selection criterion
The Chronicle's turning point analysis suggests that the quality of presidential leadership is now a legitimate factor in institutional quality. Ask how presidents are communicating about these challenges.
🏛️
Don't assume public = affordable — run the numbers
State tuition increases of 6–12% mean the public university assumption needs updating. Specific comparisons like UT Austin vs. Rice are now much closer than families expect.

Dr. Hurwitz's Bottom Line: The families who navigate this landscape successfully are the ones who stay informed and act on what they learn. Every story in this edition has a specific implication for your college planning process. Information is only as valuable as the decisions it enables.
